title: Xiaomi's Three Chips: Trading Resources for Time, Betting on an On-Device AI Paradigm Shift
dek: Xiaomi releases three Xuanjie chips in one go, aggressively betting on memory interconnect, 3D stacking, and an all-AI architecture, trading resources for time to bet on an on-device AI paradigm shift and vertical integration capabilities, but still clearly behind top-tier chip companies.
why: This episode deeply analyzes the technical choices and strategic logic behind Xiaomi's three chips. It is information-dense, with clear analogies for key technologies like memory interconnect and 3D stacking. Worth a listen for chip industry professionals and investors following Xiaomi.
who: Investors focused on Xiaomi's chip efforts, chip industry engineers, product managers, and tech professionals wanting to understand on-device AI trends.
skip: The first 3 minutes discussing the definition of self-development can be skipped; go straight to the technical analysis section.

points.h: Whether a company can make chips depends on system definition rights, not IP self-development rate
points.body: To judge whether a company can make chips, you can't just look at how many IPs it handcrafted, but how much system definition power it holds. Although Xiaomi's Xuanjie O1 uses ARM IP for CPU and GPU, the system integration and physical implementation are done by Xiaomi itself. Apple and Qualcomm are strong because they can iterate annually and continuously tape out, which is what latecomers lack most. Xiaomi doesn't have ten years to learn slowly, so it chooses an aggressive route, advancing multiple high-risk technology lines simultaneously.

points.h: The culprit behind O1's poor energy efficiency is the lack of a shared water tank
points.body: The Xuanjie O1 lacks a system-level cache (SLC), causing power consumption to be uncontrollable under high GPU load, leading to poor energy efficiency. SLC is like a shared large water tank in a community: the closer data is to the computing units, the faster the access and the lower the power consumption. The O1 has many GPU cores but limited DDR bandwidth, so many cores are waiting for data, and utilization cannot rise—this is the bandwidth wall. The O3 adds a 16MB SLC, splits it into multiple cache blocks distributed across the chip, and designs an on-chip network scheduling system to solve data consistency and access conflicts.

points.h: ARM's public bus is too generic, so Xuanjie had to build its own
points.body: ARM's public CHI+CMN solution is too generic, requiring compatibility and redundant designs, making it difficult to customize for Xuanjie. The O3 instead developed its own X-Ring unified fusion bus, compatible with CHI but defining its own interconnect protocol, with a self-developed high-speed network scheduling center and memory controller. This reduces protocol conversion overhead, and data can decide cache location and path based on needs. Xiaomi claims protocol conversion overhead is reduced by 75%, and static access latency is 82 nanoseconds, 32% lower than the O1, even lower than Apple's A19 Pro.

points.h: The compute bottleneck is shifting from matrix multiplication to vector operations
points.body: The O3 adds AI units to every subsystem—CPU, GPU, ISP, etc.—so computation happens where the data resides, reducing data movement. The NPU core count drops from 6 to 4, but Tensor compute rises to 200 Tops, because Xiaomi judges that the bottleneck for large models is shifting from matrix multiplication to vector operations like Softmax, quantization, and KV cache. The vector unit area is about the same as the Tensor unit, with 6.8 times the multiply-accumulate units of the O1, and introduces a SMT-like architecture, similar to CUDA, to handle irregular parallel tasks.

points.h: Chips and models should be defined together by the same company
points.body: Xiaomi partnered with MEMO to compress INT4 weights to 5 bits using a 5-value quantization method, with almost no loss in precision, reducing memory bandwidth and capacity requirements by 30%. The 3-billion-parameter MEMO model deployed on the O3 shows a 40% improvement in prefill performance and 45% in decode. This ability to co-define chips and models is the closed-loop advantage of vertical integration—no need to wait for others to define models before adapting.

points.h: 3nm performance is achieved by squeezing standard cells bit by bit
points.body: The O3 uses the more mature N3P process, delivering 5% performance improvement at the same power and 5%-10% power reduction at the same frequency. Xiaomi also did extensive process optimization: self-developed standard cells increased from 480 in the O1 to over 2,400, covering various chip units; compressed power supply buffer channels so power and signals route from the middle of modules, increasing transistor density by 5%. The CPU changed from 4 clusters to 3 clusters with 10 big cores, boosting single-core performance by 31% and multi-core by 60%, surpassing the A19 Pro.

points.h: Near-memory computing pushes phone memory bandwidth to 1.22TB/s
points.body: The Xuanjie O100 uses wafer-level 3D stacking: one compute wafer plus two memory wafers stacked vertically, interconnected via hybrid bonding, forming a near-memory computing architecture. It uses thousands of shorter, denser vertical connections to achieve high bandwidth, with lower energy per bit shift, similar to HBM for phones. Data: 28,762 data connections, bandwidth 1.22TB/s, far exceeding the tens of bits wide connections of traditional SoC with LPDDR. The compute layer has 14 independent cores, each with a RISC-V processor for control.

points.h: CXMT's value lies not in speed grade but in co-definition
points.body: Xiaomi partnered with CXMT to debut LPDDR6, reducing dependence on Samsung and SK Hynix. Even if CXMT provides the 10.667Gbps entry speed grade, Xiaomi can compensate for peak rate gaps through wider channels, larger SLC, and self-developed memory controllers. More importantly, the two sides jointly validate and tune from the design stage, co-defining China's mobile memory subsystem solution. For CXMT, this proves its high-speed I/O and physical layer capabilities, earning a seat at the next-generation mobile memory table.

points.h: Xiaomi is betting not on chips but on a time window
points.body: First, it bets on a paradigm shift in on-device computing: AI's weight in SoCs is increasing, phones become AI interaction gateways, and Xiaomi wants to stand in the definer's position. Second, it bets that vertical integration becomes a core competency for terminal companies: generic chips cannot meet the fragmented needs of human, car, and home scenarios, so one must master one's own computing architecture. Third, it bets on an uncertain time window: trading resources for time to compress the technology catch-up cycle, preferring to bear engineering risks rather than wait for the window to close.

points.h: Xuanjie is catching up faster, but none of the three thresholds have been crossed
points.body: Top-tier SoC companies need three capabilities: self-developed CPU/GPU microarchitecture, self-developed 5G baseband, and continuous multi-generation stable tape-outs with tens of millions of shipments. Xuanjie currently meets none of these, still clearly behind the first tier—it's just catching up faster. What truly changes the industry landscape is not a single impressive chip but the continuous iteration capability built by a group of companies. Xuanjie's greater significance is proving that Xiaomi's chip efforts haven't stopped and that it is moving forward with China's chip industry partners.

terms.def: A cache shared by multiple compute units within a chip, like a community's shared large water tank.
A wafer-level 3D stacking interconnect technology that directly connects copper pillars, offering high bandwidth and low power.
Placing storage and compute units close together to reduce data movement distance, improving bandwidth and energy efficiency.
A performance bottleneck where data movement capability becomes the limiting factor, preventing additional compute cores from being utilized.
A parallel processing architecture that can manage multiple task groups simultaneously, improving compute unit utilization.

quotes.text: To judge whether a company can really make chips, don't just stare at how many IPs it handcrafted; you should look at how much system definition power it holds.
Xiaomi is not slowly learning to make chips; it is trading resources for time, trying to build, within a limited time window, the complete capability station that a mature chip company needs.
As long as data is stored reasonably and distributed efficiently, the entire chip can benefit.
Once it succeeds, you don't have to wait for someone else to define the model, then adapt a generic chip to it, and then figure out how to stuff it into a phone.
Better to bear more engineering and R&D uncertainty than to wait until the window truly closes and regret not having moved faster.
